item.title: Resonance-engineered single-photon routing in an asymmetric Jaynes-Cummings cavity-waveguide system
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Output probability in channel 2 becomes completely energy-independent (P2=1/2 for equal-weight normalized input) when coupling parameters and input amplitudes satisfy J2=2J1 and α1=−α2.

Grade 0.441 · 2.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks” · Adam Sulieman Ibrahim Abdalla

Figure

Output routing probabilities P1, P2, and P3 versus normalized photon energy ε/ω0 for coherent two-port input states, highlighting energy-independent routing in P2 when J2=2J1 and α1=−α2.

Asks

How do coupling asymmetry, atom-cavity detuning, and coherent multichannel input state preparation jointly determine single-photon routing in a Jaynes-Cummings cavity-waveguide network?

But

Single-excitation subspace; linear waveguide dispersion; no direct interwaveguide coupling; point-like cavity-waveguide delta couplings.

Tools

real-space scattering theory · Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonian · three-channel S-matrix formalism

Abstract

We investigate single-photon scattering and routing in an asymmetric cavity-waveguide quantum electrodynamics system consisting of a Jaynes-Cummings cavity-emitter subsystem coupled to two one-dimensional waveguides. Using a real-space scattering approach, we derive an exact three-channel scattering matrix and analytical expressions for the channel-resolved scattering amplitudes. The scattering response is governed by the interplay of asymmetric cavity-waveguide coupling, atom-cavity detuning, coherent preparation of a single-photon superposition across multiple input channels, and intrinsic dissipation. Coupling asymmetry controls the relative weights of the cavity-mediated scattering pathways, whereas atom-cavity detuning modifies their spectral response. Coherent multichannel input states provide an additional phase-sensitive control of the output probabilities through interference. In particular, we identify an analytical condition, J₂=2J₁ and α₁=-α₂, under which the probability in the second output channel becomes independent of photon energy; for an equal-weight normalized input, this probability is 1/2. We further show how cavity and atomic dissipation reduce the probability remaining in the guided channels. These results provide a framework for resonance-engineered single-photon routing in asymmetric Jaynes-Cummings cavity-waveguide systems.

item.title: Differentiable Digital Twins for Optimization, Calibration, and Characterization of Neutral-Atom- and Ion-based Quantum Computers
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Introduced differentiable-digital-twin software framework `qruise-toolset` for atomic qubits, simulating single-qubit randomized benchmarking with error per Clifford of 1.11(30)×10−3 and achieving quantum volume of 24=16 with 83.1% mean heavy-output probability.

Grade 0.434 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Marco Rossignolo, Lorena C. Bianchet, Anurag Saha Roy, Shai Machnes

Figure

Heavy-output probability per circuit for 200 random four-qubit square circuits of depth 4. The cumulative mean (solid line) stays at 83.1%, exceeding the 2/3 pass threshold (dashed line) to demonstrate a quantum volume of 16.

Asks

How can atomic quantum processor dynamics and hardware control stacks be modelled and calibrated using end-to-end automatic differentiation?

But

Demonstrated primarily in numerical simulation; subject to exponential resource scaling for full state and process tomography.

Tools

automatic differentiation · quantum optimal control · digital twin modeling · Qiskit backend emulation · randomized benchmarking

Abstract

Quantum technologies based on individually controlled atoms are among the most promising platforms for scalable quantum computing, owing to their favorable coherence properties and controllability. Nonetheless, achieving reliable and high-fidelity gate operations remains challenging due to the sensitivity of these systems to noise and hardware imperfections. In this work, we introduce a comprehensive software toolset designed to model atomic quantum systems with high precision and simulate qubit gate dynamics. By integrating quantum optimal control and benchmarking techniques with automatic differentiation for efficient and accurate gradient-based optimization, the toolset enables significant improvements in gate performance. We demonstrate its capabilities through detailed case studies involving both neutral atoms and trapped ions, highlighting its effectiveness in enhancing quantum gate fidelities, and providing valuable insights for experimental implementation.

item.title: Parametric CZ Gates in a Tunable Tripod Architecture with Fixed-Frequency Superconducting Qubits
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Simulated parametric-resonance CZ gates across three pairs of fixed-frequency transmon qubits sharing one tunable coupler achieve target-subspace fidelities of 0.9943 (CZ01), 0.9834 (CZ02), and 0.9907 (CZ12). A spectator qubit initially in state |1⟩ suffers significant population distortion, transferring population or leaving the computational space.

Grade 0.415 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Chanpyo Kim, Hansol Kim, Jeongsoo Kang, Younghun Kwon

Figure

Population evolution of states |0110⟩, |0020⟩, and |0200⟩ over 500 ns under modulated coupler flux, demonstrating the parametric resonant interaction between |0110⟩ and |0020⟩.

Asks

Can selective parametric-resonance CZ gates be implemented between all pairs of fixed-frequency transmon qubits connected to a single tunable coupler using only coupler flux modulation?

But

Numerical simulation only, with three energy levels per component and no decoherence, relaxation, dephasing, or flux noise modeled; target fidelities evaluated only on the four-state subspace where the spectator qubit and coupler remain in |0⟩.

Tools

three-level transmon Hamiltonian simulation · time-dependent flux pulse optimization · virtual Z phase correction

Abstract

Efficient implementation of the operations required for quantum error correction in superconducting quantum computers requires high gate fidelity, adequate qubit connectivity, and selective control of interactions. Sharing a single coupler among multiple qubits can improve connectivity, but also requires accounting for its effects on qubits outside the target pair. In this work, we numerically investigate the feasibility of implementing parametric-resonance CZ gates in a tunable tripod structure consisting of three fixed-frequency transmon qubits connected to a single tunable coupler. We modulate the external flux applied to the coupler and optimize the pulse parameters for each qubit pair to construct CZ₀₁, CZ₀₂, and CZ₁₂ gates. We calculate the time evolution of a Hamiltonian that includes three energy levels for each circuit element and evaluate gate fidelity and leakage after virtual Z correction. The fidelities obtained for the target-pair computational blocks, whose input and output basis states have both the coupler and spectator qubit in their ground states, are 0.9943, 0.9834, and 0.9907, respectively. We also find that population preservation at the end of the gate depends on the initial state of the spectator qubit. These results demonstrate the possibility of constructing CZ operations for each qubit pair through flux modulation of a shared coupler while maintaining fixed data-qubit frequencies. They also highlight the need to evaluate performance and optimize control over the full computational space, including the spectator qubit.

item.title: Quantum-Enhanced Classical Communications for DPMZM-based NG-PON2 Systems
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — DPMZM architecture provides an SNR enhancement of approximately 6dB over conventional MZM in NG-PON2, improving BPSK BER by nearly five orders of magnitude at Ns=1.

Grade 0.408 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks” · Parvin Kumar, Sourav Banerjee, Neel Kanth Kundu, Umesh Sharma

Figure

SNR plotted against average received signal photon number Ns, showing an approximate 6dB gain for the DPMZM system over the conventional MZM architecture across the entire range.

Asks

Can quantum detection integrated with a dual-parallel Mach-Zehnder modulator architecture improve receiver sensitivity and error rates over standard MZM configurations in NG-PON2?

Before

Baseline MZM-based NG-PON2 quantum communication systems using classical or basic MZM modulation.

But

Numerical simulation and analytical model assuming shot-noise-limited detection; excludes detector loss, electronic noise, phase noise, timing jitter, and finite ADC resolution.

Tools

Dual-Parallel Mach-Zehnder Modulator (DPMZM) · Square Root Measurement (SRM) · Helstrom bound · Gram matrix analysis · Time and Wavelength Division Multiplexing (TWDM)

Abstract

This paper presents a framework for integrating quantum detection techniques into a Dual-Parallel Mach-Zehnder Modulator (DPMZM)-based Next Generation Passive Optical Network 2 (NG-PON2) communication system. We present a system model for the DPMZM-based NG-PON2 quantum communication system and characterize its signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), demonstrating its superiority over conventional MZM-based systems. We analyze the performance of various quantum modulation techniques, including binary phase-shift keying, quadrature phase-shift keying, and M-ary quadrature amplitude modulation. A comprehensive analytical framework is developed to evaluate the SNR, BER, and mutual information for both classical and quantum detection schemes within the DPMZM-based NG-PON2 quantum communication system. Our simulation results show that quantum detection significantly outperforms classical detection, and the DPMZM architecture further enhances the performance over the baseline MZM architecture by improving the effective modulation efficiency and receiver sensitivity.

item.title: A Phase-Balanced Differential Rydberg-Atom Quantum Receiver for Weak GNSS Signal Detection
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Differential Rydberg atomic receiver with local-oscillator phase balancing and inter-cell noise correlation achieves up to ~10 dB SNR gain as photon shot noise correlation approaches unity, requiring −154.5 dBm minimum detectable power at 0 dB threshold SNR.

Grade 0.394 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks” · A. K. Mandal, F. Zhang, J. H. Mikkelsen, M. Shen

Figure

Minimum detectable power Pb(min⁡) plotted against maximum outage probability Pout(max⁡) and threshold SNR γth, showing differential receiver outperforming conventional RAQR and classical GNSS architectures by 8.5 dB to 34.5 dB.

Asks

Can phase-balanced differential detection across coupled Rydberg vapor cells suppress quantum and optical shot noise to detect weak GNSS signals?

Before

Conventional single-cell RAQR required −146 dBm, 20-ms coherent HS-GNSS required −133 dBm, and conventional GNSS receiver required −120 dBm under identical 0 dB threshold SNR conditions.

But

Theoretical and simulated only; assumes perfect cell matching, precise LO phase balancing, and sustained inter-cell quantum projection and photon shot noise correlations without implementation losses or phase errors.

Tools

dual-cell Rydberg-atom electrometry · phase-balanced local oscillator control · two-mode squeezed reservoir engineering · Monte Carlo simulation (150,000 runs/point)

Abstract

This paper proposes a phase-balanced differential Rydberg atomic quantum receiver (DRAQR) for weak-signal recovery, using local-oscillator phase control to reinforce differential signal responses and a shared squeezed-reservoir model to correlate inter-cell quantum projection noise (QPN) and photon shot noise (PSN). An analytical model incorporating QPN, PSN, intrinsic thermal noise (ITN), and inter-cell correlations quantifies signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) gain, outage-constrained minimum detectable power, and bit-error rate (BER) for square M-QAM. For the evaluated settings, SNR gain reaches approximately 10~dB as PSN correlation approaches unity, with BER decreasing as correlation increases. Under Rician fading, at a 0-dB threshold SNR and maximum outage probability of 0.1, the minimum detectable power decreases from -146.95~dBm at K=1.155 to -159.98~dBm at K=2.4. Analytical results are validated against Monte-Carlo simulations over 150,000 data runs per point for receiver-performance plots.

item.title: A Tutorial on Practical QKD Post-Processing Algorithms Using a GUI-Based Simulation Framework
item.description:
Worth a look review — Practical discrete-variable QKD secret key rates track theoretical finite-key bounds closely up to 40 km, with Cascade and Polar code reconciliation extending reach to ~55 km while LDPC cuts off near 45 km.

Grade 0.391 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks” · Ushnik Nath, Neha Sharma, Ramniwas Meena, Neel Kanth Kundu

Figure

Secret key rate Rsk versus fiber transmission distance d in km. Shows Cascade, Polar, LDPC, and Winnow post-processing curves tracking below asymptotic and finite-key theoretical BB84 bounds until dropping to zero between 45 km and 55 km.

Asks

How do practical post-processing implementations of Cascade, Winnow, LDPC, and Polar codes compare against theoretical asymptotic and finite-key secret key rate bounds across realistic discrete-variable QKD channel conditions?

But

Simulated fiber transmission; discrete-variable BB84 with weak coherent pulses (mean photon number μ≈0.1 to 0.15); all protocols yield zero secret key rate for measured QBER ≥11% or μ≥0.2 at 40 km.

Tools

Actor-based server-client post-processing pipeline · Belief propagation with OSD-0 decoding (5G NR LDPC) · Polar successive cancellation decoding · Toeplitz hashing and SHAKE256 privacy amplification · Django web-based GUI

Abstract

Recent experimental demonstrations of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) have attracted significant attention for their ability to establish information-theoretically secure encryption keys for next-generation communication systems. As practical deployment accelerates, the realization of compact, scalable, and high-throughput discrete-variable (DV) QKD systems has become increasingly important. While advances in photonic integration are enabling low-size, low-weight, and low-power QKD hardware, the security and performance of these systems rely heavily on efficient post-processing techniques to generate identical, secure keys. This tutorial presents a comprehensive algorithm-level review of practical post-processing techniques for DV-QKD, with particular emphasis on information reconciliation methods based on Cascade, Winnow, low-density parity-check (LDPC), and polar codes. We also analyze the theoretical asymptotic and finite-size secret key rates (SKRs) of DV-QKD and benchmark these bounds against the practical SKRs achieved using actual post-processing algorithms. Furthermore, we present a server-client model to implement the entire QKD post-processing pipeline. The performance is evaluated in terms of QBER and SKR across various system parameters, considering the complete post-processing pipeline, including sifting, information reconciliation, privacy amplification, and authentication. This tutorial also presents a graphical user interface (GUI) for the QKD post-processing methods, enabling researchers, industry practitioners, and academic users to visualize and analyze the impact of different post-processing techniques and system parameters, such as QBER, on the SKR performance of DV-QKD systems.

This tutorial also presents a graphical user interface (GUI) for the QKD post-processing methods, enabling researchers, industry practitioners, and academic users to visualize and analyze the impact of different post-processing techniques and system parameters, such as QBER, on the SKR performance of DV-QKD systems.

item.title: Trajectory-Dependent Decoherence and Leakage During Shuttling of Multi-Spin Qubits
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Parallel shuttling minimizes decoherence and leakage at short shuttling distances, whereas sequential shuttling outperforms it over long distances across 2-, 3-, and 4-spin encodings; multi-spin fidelity loss and leakage decompose analytically into sums of at most seven pairwise spin error parameters ϵjkP.

Grade 0.386 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “trapped-ion gates, shuttling and QCCD architectures” · Yu-Ning Zhang, Aleksandr S. Mokeev, Maximilian Rimbach-Russ, David P. DiVincenzo, Viatcheslav V. Dobrovitski

Figure

Average fidelity loss 1−FXO of a 3-spin exchange-only qubit versus dimensionless shuttling length λ for sequential, parallel, and triangular protocols across channel separations δ=0.3,0.6,0.8. Parallel shuttling yields lower error at short range, whereas sequential shuttling wins at long range.

Asks

How do spatial and temporal correlations in magnetic noise affect dephasing and leakage during the shuttling of multi-spin logical qubits across different trajectories?

But

Pure dephasing via rotating-frame secular Hamiltonian (neglecting x,y noise and spin relaxation). Neglects inter-spin exchange interaction during shuttling. Assumes stationary, isotropic Gaussian noise field.

Tools

Gaussian random field model of spatio-temporal 1/f noise · mixed-unitary dephasing quantum channel · pairwise dephasing factor expansion · Pauli transfer matrix analysis

Abstract

Logical qubits encoded in collective states of multiple spins are promising building blocks for large-scale semiconductor quantum processors. As novel fault-tolerant architectures increasingly rely on qubit shuttling, understanding decoherence of the shuttled multi-spin qubits becomes crucial. We analyze fidelity and leakage of the logical qubits dephased by the spatio-temporally correlated 1/f noise, considering two-, three-, and four-spin encodings. We study different shuttling protocols and establish that for all encodings generally, parallel shuttling provides the best protection against decoherence at short distances, whereas sequential shuttling outperforms others for long-range transport (although the exact boundaries depend on the specific device parameters). We explain this common behavior in terms of the dephasing factors of pairs of the shuttled spins; we provide explicit expressions for fidelities and leakage, thus enabling experimentalists to predict performance of the multi-spin qubits from only several independently measured pairwise dephasing factors. Our results establish a connection between shuttling trajectories, noise correlations, and qubit decoherence, and provide guidance for achieving noise-resilient shuttling in scalable semiconductor quantum processors.

item.title: Raman anyon-Hubbard model in a 1D Bose lattice gas
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Raman-coupled 1D Bose lattice gases with imbalanced interactions realize a Raman anyon-Hubbard model exhibiting chiral interactions with unbounded statistical phase θ, supporting chiral bound states whose energy gap grows monotonically with θ.

Grade 0.383 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Josep Cabedo, Claudio Iacovelli, Leticia Tarruell, Alessio Celi

Figure

Two-particle energy spectrum Eq as a function of center-of-mass momentum q for Ueff=0. The continuum of scattering states is flanked by upper and lower chiral bound state bands separated by an energy gap that increases with θ.

Asks

Can a 1D lattice model exhibiting many-body anyonic physics be realized with ultracold atoms without Floquet driving?

Before

Floquet-engineered anyon-Hubbard implementations were restricted to a truncated two-particle Fock space with heating-limited coherence times.

But

Requires large band gap Ω≫t,Uσσ′, low density to neglect three-body terms, and small next-to-nearest neighbor tunneling t2≪t1.

Tools

tight-binding approximation · Floquet-free Raman coupling · perturbative band projection · two-particle exact diagonalization

Abstract

The anyon-Hubbard model is the paradigmatic lattice model of one-dimensional (1D) anyons, in which chiral interactions make bosons equivalent to particles with fractional statistics. Its continuum limit, the chiral BF theory, emerges as the low-energy description of a Raman-coupled Bose gas with imbalanced interactions. Here, we show that loading such a gas into a 1D optical lattice realizes the lattice counterpart of this theory, which we name the Raman anyon-Hubbard model. The Raman-dressed bosons acquire density-dependent Peierls phases when tunneling through occupied sites. For a small statistical phase, the model reduces to the anyon-Hubbard model, while beyond this limit it defines a distinct lattice anyon model with unbounded rather than periodic statistical interactions. Numerically, we show that the dressed gas displays the defining properties of 1D anyons, namely a density-dependent asymmetry of the ground-state momentum distribution, interaction-induced asymmetric transport and chiral bound states. Remarkably, these features are readily accessible with Raman-coupled ³⁹K atoms, opening up the experimental exploration of 1D anyons beyond the few-particle regime.
